planting.note: Give this hemiepiphytic climber a moss pole or bark totem and a loose, chunky aroid mix; it roots along the stem as it climbs and does best trained upward rather than left to trail.

directions: Provide a sturdy moss pole or bark totem for this vining species to climb, since mature leaf division only develops fully once the plant is anchored and climbing rather than sprawling loose. Juvenile leaves are simple and undivided, but as the plant matures it produces distinctive palmately compound leaves split into several narrow leaflets radiating from a central point, a dramatic transformation collectors watch for over several years. Keep the chunky, well-drained mix evenly moist but never soggy, and provide consistent warmth and high humidity to encourage steady climbing growth and leaflet development. Wipe dust from the glossy leaflets occasionally to keep them photosynthesizing efficiently in the bright, filtered light this species prefers.

planting.note: Pot in a chunky, well-aerated aroid mix and keep in bright indirect light; this Ecuadorian species is slow to establish and resents disturbance, so avoid repotting more often than necessary.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light in a chunky, fast-draining aroid mix, since this rosette-forming species is prone to root rot if kept wet at the base. Anthurium marmoratum produces broad, matte green leaves with a distinctive quilted, marbled surface pattern created by pale, slightly sunken venation set against darker leaf tissue, a texture that becomes more pronounced as the plant matures. It is a comparatively slow grower even by anthurium standards, so patience and consistent warm, humid conditions matter more than heavy fertilizing. Allow the top of the mix to dry slightly between waterings and avoid letting water sit in the developing leaf crown.

common_name: Ovate-Leaf Anthurium (Ovatifolium, Broad-Leaf Bird's Nest Anthurium)

planting.note: Grow as a large rosette specimen in bright, indirect light in a chunky, well-drained aroid mix; give it plenty of overhead room since the broad leaves spread wide as the plant matures.

directions: Site this Central and South American rosette species in bright, filtered light and a coarse, well-drained aroid mix, since dense soil around its thick roots invites rot. Anthurium ovatifolium forms broad, glossy, distinctly ovate leaves with a leathery, coriaceous texture that give the plant a bold, architectural presence quite different from the narrower strap-leaf anthuriums. As the plant matures the leaves broaden further and the rosette becomes correspondingly wide, so allow generous lateral space rather than crowding it among smaller specimens. Water when the top inch of mix dries, and maintain high humidity and warm temperatures for the fullest leaf size.

common_name: Montrichardii Anthurium (Giant Costa Rican Bird's Nest Anthurium)

planting.note: Grow as a large floor specimen in bright, indirect light in a chunky, well-drained aroid mix; this Costa Rican species eventually needs a substantial pot and generous floor space to accommodate its size.

directions: Give this large bird's-nest-type species room to spread, since mature plants form an imposing rosette of long, broad, oblong-sagittate leaves radiating from a central crown. Grow in bright, filtered light in a chunky, fast-draining aroid mix, as the thick fleshy roots are sensitive to prolonged wet conditions. Anthurium montrichardii is native to wet Costa Rican forests and appreciates consistently high humidity and warmth, growing noticeably faster than many of the smaller collector velvet-leaf species once established. Water thoroughly and allow the mix to approach dryness at the surface before watering again, and feed lightly during the growing season to support its larger leaf size.

common_name: Huixtla Anthurium (Huixtlense, Chiapas Bird's Nest Anthurium)

planting.note: Grow as a compact rosette houseplant in bright, indirect light in a chunky, well-drained aroid mix; this Mexican species stays more manageably sized than many of its larger bird's-nest relatives.

directions: Native to the humid forests of Chiapas, Mexico, this bird's-nest-type anthurium forms a tidy rosette of narrow, elliptic, dark green leaves that stays smaller and more compact than the giant bird's-nest species popular in collections. Grow in bright, indirect light in a chunky, fast-draining aroid mix, since its moderate size makes it well suited to windowsills or terrarium-adjacent shelving where larger anthuriums would not fit. Keep the mix lightly moist and provide steady warmth and humidity, and avoid letting water pool in the central crown where new leaves emerge. It is a good choice for growers who want the classic rosette form of a bird's-nest anthurium without committing to a plant that eventually outgrows the room.

planting.note: Mount or pot loosely in a coarse, fast-draining epiphytic mix and keep in bright, indirect light; this small Cuban epiphyte prefers airflow around its roots over a dense, moisture-retentive substrate.

directions: Anthurium querceum is a small Cuban epiphyte named for its distinctive lobed leaf shape, which resembles an oak leaf far more than the smooth ovate or strap-shaped foliage typical of most cultivated anthuriums. Mount it on bark or grow it loosely potted in a coarse, well-aerated epiphytic mix, since in the wild it clings to tree bark with minimal organic substrate around its roots. Provide bright, filtered light and consistently high humidity, misting or grouping it with other epiphytes to keep ambient moisture up between waterings. Let the mounting medium or mix dry noticeably between waterings, since this compact species is more forgiving of brief dryness than of constantly saturated roots.

planting.note: Grow as a large specimen plant in bright, indirect light in a chunky, well-drained aroid mix; provide a large, stable pot since this Central American species develops substantial roots and heavy leaves over time.

directions: Native to the Costa Rican and Panamanian rainforest understory, Anthurium waterburyanum develops large, glossy, heart-shaped leaves with a subtly quilted surface that catch and reflect available light, making it a striking specimen even in modest indoor lighting. Grow in bright, indirect light in a chunky, fast-draining aroid mix, since the plant's substantial root mass needs excellent aeration to avoid rot as it fills a pot. It grows steadily once established, eventually producing leaves considerably larger than many popular velvet-leaf collector species, so plan for a sizable long-term footprint. Water thoroughly when the top of the mix dries, and maintain warm temperatures and elevated humidity for the best leaf size and gloss.

common_name: Pale-Flowered Strap Anthurium (Pallidiflorum, Pendent Strap-Leaf Anthurium)

planting.note: Best grown in a hanging basket with a loose, chunky epiphytic mix in bright, indirect light; the long, narrow pendent leaves need open space below the pot to hang freely.

directions: This Central American epiphyte produces long, narrow, pendent leaves that hang gracefully downward, making it best suited to a hanging basket or elevated shelf rather than a standard upright pot. Its slender foliage is more understated than the broad velvet-leaf anthuriums, but the trailing habit and pale, subtly colored inflorescences give it a distinct quiet appeal among strap-leaf species. Grow in a loose, chunky epiphytic mix in bright, filtered light, and let the mix dry slightly at the surface between waterings to keep the fine roots well aerated. Maintain warm temperatures and high ambient humidity, and avoid handling the brittle, pendulous leaves roughly since they can crack under stress.
